item.title: Fossil bones and tools from mysterious ancient human unearthed in China
item.description: A rare combination of tools and fossils found in a Chinese cave could help scientists learn more about our mysterious extinct cousins, the Denisovans. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Timing 1080 drops to prevent predators bouncing back
item.description: While aerial 1080 drops sharply reduce numbers of rats and stoats, the predators—especially ship rats—can rebound to higher numbers within a few years. Studying 24 years of small-mammal tracking records across New Zealand's public conservation land, researchers found that the timing of these rebounds varies between regions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can AI tame torrential rain by 2050? The next frontier of weather control and forecasting
item.description: Japan has been experiencing increasingly severe damage from torrential rainfall triggered by typhoons and stationary linear rain bands. In response, an ambitious and unconventional idea is taking shape: artificially inducing heavy rainfall over the ocean to reduce extreme downpours on land. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI and big data can help logistics companies navigate supply-chain disruptions
item.description: Artificial intelligence and big-data capacity might help logistics companies withstand supply-chain disruptions by making them more agile and resilient, according to research in the International Journal of Business Performance and Supply Chain Modelling. The results are based on an analysis of responses from almost 300 logistics professionals in Indonesia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Four in five researchers report harmful interactions during geoscience fieldwork. A new survey suggests a path forward.
item.description: Fieldwork is a vital part of geoscience research, allowing scientists and students to directly observe, interact with and collect data about Earth processes that cannot be replicated in the lab. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals the surface chemistry of bio-based hybrid materials
item.description: Just a few atomic layers at the surface can strongly influence how effectively a material binds pollutants from water or how efficiently a photocatalyst responds to light. Researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Polymer Research IAP use X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to investigate the chemical states and interactions at the surfaces and interfaces of bio-based carbon materials and organic-inorganic hybrid materials. Their insights can support the targeted development of functional materials for future industrial applications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Luck or merit? Not all inequality is equally acceptable
item.description: Do you think it's fair that some people are better off financially than others? Does it perhaps matter whether those earnings stem from a lottery win or hard work? These are the kinds of questions economist Ingvild Almås of the University of Zurich is exploring. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The trapdoor spiders giving a leg up to science
item.description: WA's trapdoor spiders are endangered. Jackson Rendall is here to help—because he thinks they're "just really cool." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dementia prevention too heavily focused on personal choices, study finds
item.description: Efforts to prevent dementia may be placing too much responsibility on people's choices while overlooking the wider social and environmental conditions that shape brain health, a study has found. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Georgie Hewson

item.title: CEO politics may shape how companies compete
item.description: Decisions such as whether to cut prices, launch a product, open a new facility or make an acquisition are among those companies that consider in pursuit of a competitive edge. New research from Texas A&M University suggests a CEO's political affiliation may be associated with whether the company's overall strategy follows industry peers or charts a different course. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: Satellite imagery reveals what casualty figures alone do not tell us
item.description: How do we form a picture of conflicts? A new study published in the journal Nature explores how different types of data can be combined to give a fuller understanding of armed conflicts. Lead author Valerie Sticher uses the examples of Ukraine and Myanmar to explain the advantages and limitations of automatically analyzed satellite data. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Polarized trust in scientists driven by values, identity and politics
item.description: Trust in scientists in the UK is strong overall, with 63% indicating they have high trust in scientists in general—but a major new study finds this trust is closely shaped by people's values, identity and politics, showing some of the same patterns of division over science that have emerged in the U.S. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Eight PFAS compounds detected at low concentrations in Melbourne rain
item.description: Researchers from RMIT University and EPA Victoria detected eight PFAS compounds in rainwater samples collected in Melbourne between 2024 and 2025. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Distant sensors announced a fearsome tsunami’s birth
item.description: Nature, Published online: 10 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02809-6 Seismic data pinpoint the collapse of an underwater volcano, and reveal how the eruption triggered a destructive tsunami. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Electrical fingerprint on tiny cell particles could offer new way to spot pancreatic cancer signals
item.description: An electrical fingerprint found on tiny particles in the blood may help detect signs of pancreatic cancer that are often overlooked, according to new research from Rice University. The researchers developed a device that separates these particles based on their electrical charge, making cancer-associated signals more visible. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rising sea levels could cost Australians at least $855 billion by 2100
item.description: Rising sea levels and storm surges could cost $855 billion in economic losses across Australia by the end of the century, according to new research, the first of its kind in Australia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What really drives tourists to choose a hotel? New global study reveals the answer
item.description: Why do travelers choose one hotel over another, and what makes them return? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unconventional quantum materials could dramatically boost the search for dark matter
item.description: For decades, physicists have searched for dark matter, the invisible substance thought to make up roughly 85% of all matter in the universe. Although its gravitational influence shapes galaxies and the large-scale structure of the cosmos, dark matter has never been directly detected. Now, an international team has identified a new class of quantum materials that could dramatically improve the search for some of the lightest and most elusive forms of dark matter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: LLM use may threaten freedom of thought and equality across law, journalism and education
item.description: The Human Rights Center at UC Berkeley School of Law has released a human rights assessment of the use of large language models (LLMs) in the fields of law, journalism and education. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny salt crevices could act as miniature 'Greenhouses' for Martian microbes
item.description: We've been searching for life on Mars for a long time, but so far we've come up empty. The fundamental problem is a Catch-22 involving two of the key ingredients for life. Life as we know it needs liquid water and reasonable temperatures, both of which are available on Mars, but hardly ever at the same time. But a new paper from lead author Anna Bognar and her team at ELTE Eötvös Loránd University and the Konkoly Observatory describes a way for life to access both requirements at the same time—by hiding away in salt crystals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New insect genus and four species named for Taylor Swift and her albums
item.description: Taylor Swift is now the namesake of a genus of plant-feeding insects from Australia that were previously unknown to science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI ethics problem may lie with organizations, not engineers, study finds
item.description: AI engineers often recognize ethical risks associated with the systems they build, but many lack the authority, incentives and organizational support needed to act on them, according to new research from the University of Manchester. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Natural clay reveals a new way to control ion transport at the angstrom scale
item.description: Researchers at the National Graphene Institute have shown that naturally occurring channels within a common clay mineral can respond to pressure, voltage and pH, offering possibilities for controlling the movement of ions through extremely small, confined spaces. The study, published in Advanced Materials, focuses on vermiculite, a naturally abundant layered clay whose structure contains channels only a few angstroms high, providing naturally confined pathways through which ions can move. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Molecular surface design achieves over 100 million-fold tuning of porous liquid viscosity
item.description: Porous liquids combine permanent nanoscale cavities with fluidity, making them promising for applications like carbon dioxide capture, gas separation and other chemical processes. Their viscosity must be tailored to the intended application: Lower-viscosity liquids are easier to pump and circulate while facilitating faster heat and mass transfer, whereas higher-viscosity liquids provide greater structural stability in membrane formation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Africa's rocks hold ancient stories. We need better ways to document and protect them
item.description: From the Vredefort Dome in South Africa (the world's oldest and largest known meteorite impact structure) to the volcanic lakes of the Great Rift Valley in Kenya, Africa's landscapes hold some of Earth's oldest stories. Morocco's M'Goun UNESCO Global Geopark records more than 200 million years of geological history, while Tanzania's Ngorongoro-Lengai landscape brings together a vast caldera, an active volcano and the fossil record of Olduvai Gorge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How adoption of a new crop reshaped land use in Bronze Age Europe
item.description: A new study published in Science Advances reveals how Bronze Age communities in Central Europe adapted to changing environmental and social conditions by adopting broomcorn millet, a fast-growing, climate-resilient crop. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Molecular antennae make light-activated molecular switches more sensitive
item.description: From targeted cancer treatments to self-healing materials and microscopic robots, many emerging technologies depend on molecules that can be controlled with light. Researchers at Tohoku University have now developed a way to make these light-responsive molecules much more sensitive to visible light by using a molecular antenna. The breakthrough gives scientists better control over molecular photoswitches remotely and potentially expands their use in medicine and advanced materials. The findings are published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Beryllium signal identifies stars that have swallowed rocky planets
item.description: An international team led by researchers from the University of São Paulo (USP) in Brazil has developed an innovative method to identify stars that have consumed the planets around them. The technique detects variations in the abundance of beryllium, a relatively rare chemical element, and could open a new window into studying the evolution of planetary systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chandra uncovers 'hypersoft X-ray sources' that may solve two astrophysical puzzles
item.description: Using NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, scientists have discovered a new class of objects behaving unlike any they have seen before. Astronomers suggest these newly spotted objects in other galaxies may help solve not one, but two long-standing questions in astrophysics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration
item.description: We're already nostalgic! Relive the excitement and joy from Roman’s launch with the most recent episode of NASA’s Curious Universe podcast, now available. They’re also diving into next steps for the... Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Terbium's elusive plus-4 form emerges under ordinary lab conditions, opening possibilities for rare-earth metals
item.description: Chemists in a new study led by the University of Iowa report they have isolated and described in detail an atypical state of the rare-earth metal terbium, an advance that could expand its use in quantum technologies, including computing and advanced sensors. The study, "Structural and spectroscopic characterization of a Tb(IV) polyoxometalate," is published in the journal Nature Communications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cacao genetics could help breeders reduce heavy metal levels in cocoa beans
item.description: Cadmium is a naturally occurring, toxic heavy metal found in many soils across Latin America and the Caribbean, where cacao trees are widely cultivated. It makes its way into cocoa seeds, called beans, that are roasted and made into chocolate, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)—but some cacao varieties take up less of the toxic element than others. An international team of researchers, including Penn State scientists, found genetic differences in how two varieties managed cadmium uptake and facilitated the metal's movement throughout the plant. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How seeds decide whether to wake up in salty soil
item.description: Researchers have discovered a system that helps seeds survive when there is too much salt in the soil. The system helps young germinating embryos keep the right balance of sodium and potassium as they begin to grow. Understanding how it works could eventually help scientists develop crops that grow better in salty soils. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: These bacteria can change their diet to survive inside the body
item.description: The human body fights staph infections by starving it of essential nutrients. Staph, it turns out, is remarkably good at changing what's on the menu. Staphylococcus aureus—the infamous agent behind MRSA and most staph infections—needs sulfur to build proteins and other materials essential for survival. In a new Michigan State University study, published in the Journal of Bacteriology, researchers found the bacterium can adjust its diet depending on what sources remain available. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers chart new course for AI-powered biomedical discoveries
item.description: University of Missouri researchers are paving the way as artificial intelligence transforms biomedical research. A team from the College of Engineering and collaborators recently published one of the most comprehensive reviews to date of an emerging AI approach for biology known as flow matching. The work, published in Nature Machine Intelligence, provides scientists around the world with a roadmap for applying the technology to accelerate drug discovery, precision medicine and other biomedical advances. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: American women in communities with ample broadband access lose less time waiting for services, reducing time poverty
item.description: Drawing on 14 years of data, we examined whether access to broadband internet could improve Americans' use of time and found that a 10% increase in broadband adoption across a community corresponds to a 1.19% reduction in waiting time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Europe's forests are still standing, but many are losing the ability to recover
item.description: A forest can look intact from the roadside and still have lost much of its capacity to bounce back. That gap between appearance and function is at the center of a new policy brief published by eLTER, the European research infrastructure for long-term ecosystem, critical zone and socio-ecological research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Europe may finally have found a space entrepreneur who is meeting the moment
item.description: "We will not be relevant without a massive rocket at a massive cadence." Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: How 'positive' stress could improve the welfare of zoo animals
item.description: Pelicans have resided in St James's Park, London, for 360 years. But the current flock has been a summer sensation because of the first chicks to hatch in the park's history. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fossil ribs reveal new secrets about ichthyosaur swimming technique
item.description: Ichthyosaurs ruled the oceans for 150 million years during the Mesozoic Era. Their fish-shaped bodies were built for high speeds. In that context, it is normally an advantage to be as light as possible. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Adds Relativity Space’s Terran R to Launch Services Contract
item.description: A NASA Launch Services (NLS) II contract has been awarded by the agency to Relativity Space Inc., and its Terran R launch service in accordance with the contract’s on-ramp provision. The Terran R launch service will be available to NASA’s launch services to use for future missions. The NLS II contracts are multiple-award, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contracts […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: Electrochemical system extracts pure hydrogen from ammonia at substantially lower temperatures
item.description: As a liquid that is easily stored and transported, ammonia (NH3) is an attractive carrier for hydrogen, which is used in fuel cells, semiconductor manufacturing, chemical processing and other applications. However, breaking ammonia into hydrogen and nitrogen typically requires high temperatures, and the resulting gas mixture must undergo additional purification before the hydrogen can be used in many applications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Having compassion for oneself is linked to well-being, study finds
item.description: Caring for others without caring for oneself is associated with lower levels of well-being and may not be sustainable, a new study found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What to know about Europe's push to compete in space
item.description: Key figures from Europe's space industry and other international players have converged on Paris to discuss how to advance the continent's ambitions in a global market dominated by the United States. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why customers accept price rises
item.description: Piling sight, sound, touch, smell and taste into digitally enhanced tourist attractions does not automatically make visitors more engaged, according to research from the University of Surrey. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 3D magnetic-field control reveals new way to tune spin textures
item.description: (Fe0.63Ni0.3Pd0.07)3P, or FNPP, is a magnetic material that exhibits complex magnetic structures even at room temperature. This makes the material of interest for spintronics, a field that could enable data processing with significantly lower energy consumption. One potential application is novel magnetic memory devices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Artemis II moonshot commander and pilot are hanging up their astronaut suits at NASA
item.description: The two NASA astronauts who led the Artemis II moonshot earlier this year are stepping away from spaceflight. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Estuary water quality trends have $100M implications, researchers find
item.description: Estuaries across the United States are facing the same trends of warming waters, algal growth and declining oxygen concentrations that threaten water quality and fish populations, regardless of geographic location, according to new research led by a Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) faculty member. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reports of drug seizures by police rose during first year of decriminalization, study finds
item.description: People in Vancouver experienced an increase in police drug seizures during the first year of British Columbia's drug decriminalization pilot project, according to a Simon Fraser University study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Five‑metal alloy: Scientists create ultra‑stable catalyst for fuel cells
item.description: Hydrogen-powered cars, power stations and portable chargers all rely on fuel cells. At the heart of each fuel cell is a catalyst that speeds up the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity and water. These catalysts are typically made of platinum—which costs nearly as much as gold. Researchers from Southern Federal University, together with colleagues from Skoltech (part of the VEB.RF Group), the Institute of Catalysis of the Siberian Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences, and Bauman Moscow State Technical University, have found a way to make this key component both… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Discontinuity and disorder: Explaining the luminosity bump in evolved stars
item.description: Toward the end of their lives, low-mass stars undergo an abrupt dip in brightness, also known as the luminosity bump. While the endpoint of this bump is well understood, its onset has remained elusive. Now, in a paper published by The Astrophysical Journal Letters, Saskia Hekker, leader of the Theory and Observations of Stars group at the Heidelberg Institute for Theoretical Studies (HITS), finds that entropy is the key driver of the bump. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Maria Thibeault ha comentado: I see an anatomically correct heart
item.description: Hey, neighbor Did you know our home galaxy — the Milky Way — has smaller galaxies that orbit around it? The biggest one, called the Large Magellanic... Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Long-lost fish species rediscovered in another section of the Inn River
item.description: The Danube gudgeon had been considered extinct in the Inn River for more than 100 years. Only a few years ago, the highly endangered species was rediscovered there. Now, researchers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM) have documented the fish in another section of the Inn. The finding emerged from a joint research project with hydropower operator VERBUND examining the effects of nature-like fishways on fish populations and river ecology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Helium measurements clarify conditions seconds after the Big Bang
item.description: New observations of the composition of distant galaxies offer insights into the earliest phases of the universe and confirm decades of scientific understanding of the elements and particles produced by the Big Bang, according to a new study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Whose space is it? Europe scrambles as US rules satellite race
item.description: With the digital age comes the scramble for minerals below us and the scramble to master the heavens above us. Donald Trump wants a thousand rocket launches a year and with SpaceX’s reusable modules leading the way, the United States towers over the competition. It’s why for instance Ukraine’s president has to beg Elon Musk to use his Starlink low orbit satellite system to take out the Russian cruise missile launchers. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: François PICARD

item.title: You can't shield kids from scary news—here's what 'Sesame Street' and other children's shows did after 9/11
item.description: On back-to-school night in 2005, I eagerly entered my youngest child's first-grade classroom. The walls were festooned with brightly colored responses to the prompt: "Draw something you remember." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI reveals new class of cellular 'off switch' linked to cancer pathways
item.description: Cornell researchers have used artificial intelligence to uncover a previously unknown way cells control how proteins move inside them, a process essential for growth, communication and movement that is often disrupted in cancer. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Chandra Unveils Mysterious X-Ray Objects
item.description: Using NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, scientists have discovered a new class of objects behaving unlike any they have seen before. Astronomers suggest these newly spotted objects in other galaxies may help solve not one, but two long-standing questions in astrophysics. These mysterious objects give off unusually low-energy X-rays but intense levels of ultraviolet radiation. This […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Newly Discovered Plant-Eating Insects Named After Taylor Swift
item.description: Taylor Swift, the award-winning billionaire singer and songwriter, is getting a new honor: The megastar is the namesake of several recently discovered species of plant-feeding insects from Australia. Researchers at the University of California, Riverside have named the new species of insect after Swift. A paper describing the 12 new species was published in the […] Fuente: Variety.
item.dc:creator: Todd Spangler

item.title: The two NASA astronauts who led the Artemis II moonshot earlier this year are leaving spaceflight behind.
item.description: The two NASA astronauts who led the Artemis II moonshot earlier this year are leaving spaceflight behind. APNEWS.COM Artemis II moonshot commander and pilot are hanging up their astronaut suits at NASA Fuente: The Associated Press.

item.title: Body-related TikTok content linked to self-objectification and mood
item.description: Viewing "thinspiration" content on TikTok increases self-objectification and worsens mood, while viewing body-positive content also increases self-objectification but is linked to a more positive mood, according to a new study published in PLOS One by Samantha Jones of Western University, Canada, and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Here, There and Everywhere': The Beatles have permeated research papers across academic disciplines
item.description: More than 3,000 scientific article titles across disciplines have made use of Beatles song titles and lyrics, according to a study published in PLOS One by Gabriel Budel of Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands and colleagues. This analysis is an unprecedentedly large-scale, cross-disciplinary account of how the Beatles have left their mark on scientific writing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fossils from embryo to adult suggest how an enigmatic, bird-like troodontid dinosaur grew
item.description: Analysis of fossilized remains from dinosaurs known as troodontids reveals how one species' hip and leg bones may have developed over its lifespan, from embryo to adult—with potential implications for resolving longstanding taxonomic challenges. David Varricchio of Montana State University, U.S., and Heath Caldwell of North Carolina State University, U.S., present their findings in the journal PLOS One on Sept. 9, 2026. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Asian elephants can resist impulsive behavior, researchers find
item.description: Researchers at the CUNY Graduate Center and Hunter College have found that Asian elephants can suppress impulsive behaviors and adjust their actions when circumstances change—a cognitive ability that may help explain the animals' sophisticated problem-solving skills and social behavior. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: JWST discovers that Chariklo's invisible rings are changing
item.description: Until just over a decade ago, ring systems were thought to be exclusive to the giant planets of the solar system, such as Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. However, in 2013, a small body barely 250 kilometers (155 miles) in diameter, located at nearly 17 times the Earth–sun distance, joined this small group. The object is Chariklo, a small body orbiting between Saturn and Uranus, around which astronomers discovered two dense rings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ice Age origins of one of humanity's oldest drug habits discovered
item.description: A team of Griffith University archaeologists has uncovered evidence that humans were using mind-altering substances much earlier than previously supposed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Decades-old DNA mystery solved after strands are captured zipping together for the first time
item.description: Researchers have captured the moment two DNA molecules zip together, overcoming their identical negative charges to pair up and revealing a mechanism that has puzzled scientists for more than 20 years. Using high-powered atomic force microscopy, scientists at the University of Sheffield and the University of York directly imaged two DNA double helices locking together, marking the first time this fundamental biological process has been visualized. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Liquid gold: Could we turn our urine into fertilizer?
item.description: For thousands of years, human urine has had real value. After our bodies absorb nutrients from our food, they excrete the rest—mainly via urine. An adult produces about 500 liters (132 gallons) a year. This liquid gold is very rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, three nutrients vital for plant growth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Survey shows public confidence in Fauci declines since spring but still exceeds RFK Jr.
item.description: Americans' confidence in Dr. Anthony Fauci as a source of trustworthy public health information declined over the four months from April to August 2026 in a survey conducted after he appeared before the U.S. Senate Homeland Security Committee but declined to answer its questions, invoking his Fifth Amendment protection against self-incrimination. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The Anthropocene was rejected as a geological epoch—but the idea is still changing how we see the world
item.description: The Anthropocene became part of the zeitgeist after Nobel laureate Paul Crutzen launched the idea in 2000. This is the notion that a crescendo of human impacts has recently propelled Earth out of the relatively stable climatic conditions of the Holocene epoch, during which human civilization developed and flourished, to produce a new kind of planet. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The surprising place where giant dinosaurs incubated their eggs
item.description: Finding a fossilized dinosaur egg is exceptionally rare, but finding a stash of more than 250 shell fragments in the chilly southern reaches of the planet is even more surprising. The discoveries come from southernmost Patagonia in Argentina, where giant, long-necked titanosaurs roamed toward the end of the dinosaur era. Previous egg discoveries suggested that these massive beasts usually nested much farther north. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Canada's last epishelf lake is gone for good, study confirms
item.description: Canada's last epishelf lake drained into the Arctic Ocean following the 2020 breakup of the Milne Ice Shelf and will not recover, a new study confirms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When benefit corporations get certified, is it 'greenwashing' in stereo?
item.description: The term "benefit corporation" is becoming increasingly familiar as a label for companies with a hybrid commitment to the social good and profit-making. Interestingly, the term itself has taken on a hybrid meaning. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Restoring Australia's she-oaks means listening to Indigenous knowledges
item.description: In Australia, many Indigenous communities have connections and stories linked to the she-oak. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny 2D cracks creep through materials before triggering sudden fracture, experiments reveal
item.description: We have all seen something suddenly break: a phone screen cracks, a plastic object snaps or a piece of glass shatters. To our eyes, the failure seems to happen all at once. But what if the most important part of the break happens long before the final snap? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The 'costly son' hypothesis: Why bigger sons may make births riskier across species
item.description: A new comparative review, published in The Anatomical Record, examines factors that may lead to birth complications among humans and other mammals. The study suggests that fetal sex may play an important role in risky births in humans and several other species. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Layer-based design offers new route to topological magnets
item.description: Topological quantum materials combine unusual electronic states with properties such as magnetism or superconductivity, offering possibilities for future electronics and quantum technologies. Researchers at Tohoku University have now shown that changing the number of layers in a crystal can provide a systematic way to design topological magnets. The work is published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Forever chemicals break apart into fluoride under UV treatment, revealing a cleanup roadmap
item.description: UC Riverside environmental engineers have identified key chemical reactions that occur when ultraviolet light is used to destroy "forever chemical" pollutants in water, providing a roadmap for developing more effective cleanup technologies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: UK subsidies for land-based seafood farming would boost tree-planting policy
item.description: Subsidies for emerging technology that allows seafood to be produced on land would boost the UK's food security and deliver significant climate benefits, new research shows. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How 2 US, European Satellites Are Studying Hurricanes During El Niño
item.description: Last November, NASA and its European partners launched the Sentinel-6B satellite to improve hurricane forecasts, help protect infrastructure, and benefit commercial industries, including shipping. The satellite now is flying 30 seconds behind its predecessor, Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich. Both satellites are providing precise sea level height measurements during what oceanographers expect to be a historic El […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Carney

item.title: Project digitally recreates a buried World War I battlefield
item.description: Imagine walking through a World War I excavation site—not wading through mud-filled trenches, but navigating a digital landscape rich with history, artifacts and human stories. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How we manage and engage with horses may shape their personality
item.description: A new study reveals that horse personality is not only a matter of genetics, age or breed but also systematically linked to how horses are housed, ridden and cared for, and to the quality of the relationship they share with their owners. The findings underscore the importance of everyday management decisions for equine personality and welfare. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: "Expertos de Anthropic advierten que la IA podría acabar con los humanos": 'Axios'
item.description: Tres investigadores de Anthropic expresaron escalofriantes preocupaciones sobre la inteligencia artificial fuera de control. 'Axios' recoge sus advertencias que apuntan a que la IA podría destruir a la humanidad en esta década. El medio explica que hay un dilema entre los gigantes tecnológicos: frenar su desarrollo y quedar atrás o avanzar en esta competencia y arriesgarse a perder el control. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: Patricio Peralta

item.title: Artemis II Crew at NASA Marshall
item.description: The crew of NASA’s Artemis II mission – NASA astronauts Christina Koch, Victor Glover, and Reid Wiseman and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen – visited Huntsville, Alabama, Sept. 1, 2026, where they met with the NASA workforce at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center. The event gave the crew an opportunity to share firsthand […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Physics-aware benchmark reveals why similar materials AI models can predict thermal conductivity differently
item.description: Material properties such as sound insulation, resistance to extreme heat and thermal expansion originate from how the zillions of microscopic building blocks (nuclei and electrons) interact at equilibrium and respond to perturbations. Atoms are typically about one ten-billionth of a meter across, so there can be a lot of parts to keep track of—a task that is complicated at the quantum-mechanical level, where particles are neither here nor there until observed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The Future We Choose: New Beyond Blue report explores the forces shaping the next decade of mental health in Australia
item.description: Beyond Blue has launched "The Future We Choose: Mental health support in Australia through the next decade of change," a new strategic foresight report by Australia's national science agency, CSIRO, exploring how mental health in Australia may evolve over the next decade and the choices that could help shape a stronger, more connected and resilient future. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New AI model for DNA learns from evolution to unlock secrets of the human genome
item.description: More than two decades after scientists first sequenced the entire human genome—all 3 billion base pairs, of DNA code—the meaning of much of this code remains a mystery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Petrochemical industry emissions could climb 50% by 2050, global mapping suggests
item.description: Carbon emissions from the petrochemical industry could increase by 50% by 2050, according to new research from the University of Sheffield. The study, published in Nature Sustainability, provides the most detailed data to date on emissions from one of the world's biggest emitters of carbon dioxide. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: White is more than a color: How nature inspired a new sustainable way to make white, water-repellent materials
item.description: Look closely at Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa, one of Japan's most iconic masterpieces. The brilliant white of the waves, snow on Mount Fuji and clouds above contain no white pigment. Instead, their whiteness comes from the way light scatters off the unprinted fibers of the washi paper itself. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: First Denisovan forearm bone discovered in southwest China
item.description: Scientists have discovered various Denisovan remains in Southwest China dating to the late Middle Pleistocene, including the first Denisovan radius—one of two long bones in the forearm. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: As African space race heats up, Senegal pursues homemade satellites
item.description: Senegalese engineers in hairnets and white gloves are carefully assembling a nanosatellite at a French lab—another step toward fostering their own space industry back home. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reading app boosts kids' literacy
item.description: A new Flinders University study of primary school children shows a science-based digital phonics reading app can accelerate early reading while helping teachers quickly identify students needing extra support. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 66.5-million-year-old trackway captures adult T. rex at walking pace
item.description: Scientists from the Denver Museum of Nature & Science and Liverpool John Moores University in England have discovered the first adult T. rex trackway, providing insights into how this emblematic predator moved. The findings are published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Anak Krakatau erupts, disrupting 300,000 travelers as 1883 disaster looms large
item.description: Indonesia's Mount Anak Krakatau has erupted again this week, sending plumes of volcanic ash high into the sky and disrupting hundreds of flights. More than 300,000 passengers have been affected. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hidden microplastic pollution in Swiss waters uncovered
item.description: Microplastics are plastic particles smaller than 5 millimeters that originate either from manufactured products or from the breakdown of larger plastic items. They can now be found everywhere, from oceans and rivers to soils and indoor air. Because most plastics degrade very slowly, these particles can remain in the environment for decades or centuries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US scrambles to match China’s air-breathing hypersonic missiles with Darpa programme
item.description: A year after China unveiled the world’s first operational air-breathing hypersonic missiles, the United States is launching a programme to double down on developing similar weapons. The US Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency (Darpa) will bring contractors together later this month to lay out what it wants from the Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile, with air-breathing propulsion at the heart of the project, according to the agency’s website. Unlike rocket-powered missiles,... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ling Xin

item.title: More than numbers: First global dataset shows who is immigrating
item.description: As countries compete for skilled workers and grapple with aging populations and labor shortages, understanding who is moving across borders is increasingly important. A new study provides the first global data set of immigration composition disaggregated simultaneously by age, sex and educational attainment, offering a new basis for tracking brain gain and brain drain and improving population projections. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient DNA reveals 1,000 years of human-environment interactions at Crawford Lake
item.description: An international team of scientists has recreated a 1,000-year timeline documenting ecological changes and human impact on the area surrounding Crawford Lake, the famed location of the proposed Anthropocene. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Heat forces French Champagne makers to stiffen their drink
item.description: Drinking this year's champagne might cause a heftier headache as France's record heat waves force some producers to increase alcohol levels, industry officials said Wednesday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find a bone-building switch that could fight osteoporosis
item.description: An experimental compound called AP503 significantly strengthened bones in mice by activating GPR133, a receptor that boosts bone formation while slowing bone loss. Because the same treatment has also been linked to stronger muscles, researchers see intriguing potential for combating age-related decline and osteoporosis. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Ancient bones reveal that cannibalism took different forms in Neolithic Spain
item.description: Cannibalism was sometimes on the Neolithic menu, as numerous archaeological discoveries have revealed. But while ancient human bones show the practice took place, far less evidence exists about the forms it may have taken or why people occasionally consumed one another. Was it to stave off hunger during times of desperation? Did different tribes eat their defeated enemies? Or was cannibalism part of complex rituals? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In North Carolina, a race is on to restore critical peatland before it dries up or is destroyed
item.description: The birds are up with the sunrise—warblers, flycatchers, sparrows and towhees calling across the treetops. Deer browse on tender buds emerging from dense shrubs. Black bears scrounge for roots, insects and other edibles. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Could quantum protocols make electronic voting more secure?
item.description: Electronic voting, the use of electronic systems to cast, record or count votes, could potentially simplify the process of electing new political leaders or other representatives. While some countries have already started using internet-connected devices or electronic voting machines at polling stations, the trustworthiness, security and anonymity of electronic voting systems are still widely debated. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Soft X-ray absorption spectroscopy of organic molecules in organic solvents for applying organic reactions
item.description: In research published in the journal Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, the electronic structures of organic molecules containing sp2-hybridized carbons in organic solvents were studied using C K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), termed "Soft-XAS-OS." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI ‘Could Kill Us All,’ Warns Anthropic Researcher as He Quits the Company: AI Companies Are ‘Gambling With Our Lives’
item.description: Multiple current and former Anthropic employees warned — and admitted — on Tuesday that the researchers building new AI models believe the technology could lead to humanity’s destruction by the end of the decade, reflecting the industry’s frenzy over reining in rapid development. Jacob Coxon, a former AI researcher at Anthropic, wrote on X that he […] Fuente: Variety.
